evidence: Quint. 1.4.19: noster sermō articulōs nōn dēsīderat
terms.comment: English “the” is not translated: “the countryman waits for the river to run out” is rūsticus exspectat dum dēfluat amnis. Where it matters which one is meant, Latin says so with a pronoun (below); otherwise the context decides.

terms.grammar: demonstrative, after a name or noun
evidence: Cic. Imp. Pomp. 22: Mēdēa illa (Lewis & Short)
Cic. Sen. 50: honestum illud Solōnis est (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: The “the” of something everyone knows: Xenophōn, Sōcraticus ille, Xenophon, the pupil of Socrates (Cic. de Or. 2.58, Lewis & Short).

evidence: Cic. Amic. 80: is quī est tamquam alter īdem
Hor. Epod. 2.1: beātus ille quī procul negōtiīs
terms.comment: “The man who”, “the thing that”: is quī, id quod; with more weight, ille quī.

phrases.latin: rūsticus exspectat dum dēfluat amnis; at ille lābitur et lābētur in omne volūbilis aevum
phrases.english: the countryman waits for the river to run out; but on it glides, and will glide, rolling on for ever

phrases.latin: pendentem summā capream dē rūpe vidēbis: cāsūram spērēs; dēspicit illa canēs
phrases.english: you will see the goat hanging from the top of the cliff; you would expect it to fall; it looks down on the dogs

phrases.latin: beātus ille quī procul negōtiīs, ut prīsca gēns mortālium
phrases.english: happy the man who, far from business, like the first race of men …
